body:
Why negotiations began

By 1930, the Civil Disobedience Movement had caused widespread political unrest, while British repression had led to large numbers of arrests. The government was also considering constitutional reforms for India. These circumstances created an opportunity for negotiations between the Viceroy and the Congress leadership.

The British government organised Round Table Conferences in London to discuss India's constitutional future. The First Round Table Conference took place from November 1930 to January 1931. The Indian National Congress did not participate because it was engaged in civil disobedience and many of its leaders were imprisoned.

The Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931

Gandhi and Viceroy Lord Irwin reached an agreement on 5 March 1931. It is known as the Gandhi-Irwin Pact, or Delhi Pact.

The agreement provided for the suspension of the Civil Disobedience Movement in exchange for specified concessions by the colonial government.

Commitments by the Congress

  • Discontinue organised violations of colonial laws as part of the movement.
  • Stop campaigns for non-payment of land revenue and other legal dues.
  • End the organised political boycott of British goods as a means of pressure during the negotiations.
  • Participate in further constitutional discussions through the Round Table Conference process.

Concessions by the government

  • Release prisoners detained for activities connected with civil disobedience that did not involve violence or incitement to violence.
  • Withdraw ordinances and declarations against organisations made specifically in connection with the movement.
  • Withdraw pending prosecutions connected with civil disobedience that did not involve violence or incitement to violence, excluding cases against soldiers or police for disobeying orders, and remit fines that had not yet been collected.
  • Restore certain seized or confiscated property that remained in government possession; illegally possessed goods were excluded, and property attached for unpaid dues could be withheld if the defaulter persisted in refusing payment.
  • Permit residents of villages immediately adjoining salt-producing areas to collect or make salt for domestic use or sale within those villages, but not for sale to or trade with people outside those villages.
  • Allow peaceful, non-coercive picketing within the limits of ordinary law, without intimidation, obstruction or hostile demonstrations.

These were conditional concessions. They did not amount to a general cancellation of all punishments or a complete removal of colonial restrictions.

What the pact did not grant

The agreement did not grant India complete independence. It also did not abolish the salt tax or the general salt law. The government allowed limited local salt collection and manufacture but retained the wider salt regulations.

Furthermore, the prisoner-release provisions did not cover people convicted of violent offences or incitement to violence. Gandhi raised complaints about police conduct but did not obtain the public inquiry he had sought.

Important distinction: Limited permission to make or collect salt in specified coastal villages was not the same as abolition of the British salt monopoly and tax throughout India.

The Karachi Congress session of 1931

The Congress met at Karachi in March 1931 under the presidency of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. The session endorsed the Gandhi-Irwin settlement and authorised Gandhi to represent the Congress in the next Round Table Conference.

The session is also associated with resolutions concerning fundamental rights and economic policy. These discussions formed part of the Congress's wider vision for an independent India, even though the immediate negotiations had not secured independence.

The Second Round Table Conference

Gandhi travelled to London in 1931 to attend the Second Round Table Conference, held during September–December 1931. He attended as the sole representative of the Indian National Congress. Other Indian political and community representatives also attended, so Gandhi was not the only Indian delegate.

The conference discussed constitutional reforms, including the future structure of government and the political representation of different communities. Major disagreements remained unresolved, particularly over minority representation and safeguards. The negotiations therefore failed to produce an agreement acceptable to the principal parties.

Why the suspension was temporary

Gandhi returned to India disappointed by the failure of the negotiations. Meanwhile, the new Viceroy, Lord Willingdon, pursued a more repressive policy towards nationalist activities. This deteriorating situation contributed to the decision to resume civil disobedience in 1932.

Prelims focus

  • 5 March 1931: Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
  • First Round Table Conference, 1930–1931: Congress did not participate.
  • Karachi Congress, 1931: Presided over by Vallabhbhai Patel; endorsed the settlement.
  • Second Round Table Conference, 1931: Gandhi attended as the sole Congress representative.
  • Prisoner release: Applied to specified non-violent civil-disobedience offences, not all political convictions.
  • Trap: The pact permitted restricted local salt-making but did not abolish the salt tax.

[British House of Commons, Hansard, 5 March 1931, vol. 249, cols. 595–601, 'Conversations Between the Governor-General of India and Mr. Gandhi', especially clauses 3–20, accessed 21 November 2026; Indian National Congress, 'Synopsis of Plenary Sessions from 1885 to 2018', 45th Session, Karachi, 1931, accessed 21 November 2026; UK Parliament, '1931 Indian Round Table Conference', parliamentary collections, accessed 21 November 2026; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, 'Nationalism in India', printed pp. 64–65; Rajghat Samadhi Committee, 'Life Events of Mahatma Gandhi', entries for 1931, accessed 21 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A timeline shows Congress absent from the First Conference, the pact enabling Gandhi’s attendance at the Second, and Civil Disobedience resuming after unresolved talks.
pictures.caption: Congress participation differed between the First and Second Round Table Conferences.

title: Gandhi-Irwin Pact and the Round Table Conferences

body:
The movement resumes in 1932

The Gandhi-Irwin Pact had interrupted civil disobedience, but it had not resolved the central demand for complete independence. After the unsuccessful Second Round Table Conference in 1931 and renewed repression in India, Gandhi and the Congress decided to resume the movement in January 1932.

The colonial government responded firmly. Congress organisations faced restrictions, leaders were arrested and public meetings and demonstrations were suppressed. Gandhi and other important nationalist leaders were again imprisoned.

The renewed campaign continued under more difficult conditions than the initial mobilisation of 1930. Some groups had become discouraged, and prolonged imprisonment and repression weakened the capacity to organise mass protests.

Why the movement lost momentum

Several developments reduced the strength of civil disobedience during its later phase:

  • Severe repression: Arrests and restrictions disrupted local leadership and organisation.
  • Uneven social support: Some rich peasants were disappointed that revenue demands had not been reduced; business support also became less uniform.
  • Economic hardship: Continued agricultural distress made sustained participation difficult for many households.
  • Differences in political priorities: Various communities and organisations placed different demands before the national leadership.
  • Changes in Congress activity: Constructive work, questions of social equality and debates over constitutional participation received increasing attention.

The mass phase weakened during 1933, although forms of individual civil disobedience continued. The movement was brought to a close in 1934.

What the movement achieved

It challenged the legitimacy of colonial laws

By breaking the salt law openly, Gandhi demonstrated that a law could be resisted as unjust without using violence. When similar acts occurred across the country, the protest challenged the colonial government's expectation of obedience.

It expanded participation in nationalist politics

Peasants, women, students, merchants and other groups participated in different ways. Their involvement extended nationalist politics beyond formal political organisations and legislative debates.

The participation of women in salt-making, picketing, demonstrations and imprisonment was particularly important. It increased their visibility in public political life, even though equal authority within national organisations remained a separate challenge.

It connected national freedom with everyday grievances

The salt tax linked the demand for independence to an essential daily necessity. Campaigns against land revenue, chaukidari taxes and forest restrictions similarly connected colonial rule to problems experienced by people in their own localities.

It compelled the government to negotiate

The Gandhi-Irwin Pact demonstrated that the colonial government could be brought into direct negotiations with Congress leadership during a mass movement. Nevertheless, the agreement involved limited concessions rather than recognition of India's complete independence.

What the movement did not achieve immediately

The Civil Disobedience Movement did not end British rule in 1930, 1931 or 1934. The salt tax was not generally abolished under the Gandhi-Irwin Pact, and the wider disputes over constitutional power and political representation remained unresolved.

Its importance therefore lies in the growth of organised anti-colonial resistance, the political experience gained by participants, and the demonstration that a familiar everyday grievance could become the starting point for a nationwide freedom struggle.

Chronology of the complete movement

The main sequence begins with the Congress's declaration of Purna Swaraj in December 1929 and the Independence Day pledge on 26 January 1930. Gandhi started the Dandi March on 12 March and broke the salt law on 6 April 1930. The movement then spread, and Gandhi was arrested on 5 May 1930.

The Gandhi-Irwin Pact suspended civil disobedience on 5 March 1931. Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference later that year, but the negotiations failed. The Congress renewed civil disobedience in 1932, and the campaign eventually ended in 1934.

Keep the movements separate: The Non-Cooperation Movement was withdrawn in 1922; the Civil Disobedience Movement began in 1930, was suspended in 1931, resumed in 1932 and ended in 1934. The Quit India Movement was a different campaign launched in 1942.

Prelims focus

  • 1930: Salt Satyagraha began and the Civil Disobedience Movement spread nationwide.
  • 1931: Gandhi-Irwin Pact and Second Round Table Conference.
  • 1932: Civil Disobedience Movement resumed after the failure of negotiations.
  • 1933: Mass mobilisation weakened, with individual civil disobedience continuing.
  • 1934: Civil Disobedience Movement ended.
  • Trap: The movement was historically significant, but neither the Dandi action nor the Gandhi-Irwin Pact immediately brought complete independence.

[NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, 'Nationalism in India', printed pp. 63–69; IGNOU, Indian National Movement, Unit 15, sections 15.6–15.9, covering negotiations, renewed agitation and assessment; INFLIBNET, 'Salt Satyagraha and Civil Disobedience Movement', sections on withdrawal and historical significance, accessed 21 November 2026; Indian National Congress, 'All India Congress Committee Meetings, May 1934 to April 1936', Patna proceedings of May 1934, resolution on suspension of civil resistance; Rajghat Samadhi Committee, Government of India, 'Life Events of Mahatma Gandhi', entries for 1930–1934, accessed 21 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Timeline of Civil Disobedience from its 1930 launch through suspension, resumption and 1934 end, separated from Non-Cooperation and Quit India.
pictures.caption: One-glance revision of the main dates, phases and results of the movement.

title: The Second Phase, Withdrawal and Historical Impact of Civil Disobedience
